descripcion: The present perfect connects the past to now; the past simple describes a finished, closed time. At B1 the clearest rule is: if there's a finished time word (yesterday, last year), use the past simple. If the time is still open (this year, ever, never), use the present perfect.

ejemplos.texto: I visited Paris last year with my family.
I've visited Paris twice, but never in winter.

notas: Yesterday, last year and ago always take the past simple, never the present perfect.
Ever and never usually go with the present perfect, for life experience.
When always takes the past simple, even for a recent event.

contraste.es: Spanish uses the pretérito perfecto (he visitado) for open time in much of Spain, but the indefinido almost always in Latin America, even for open time. Latin American Spanish speakers therefore tend to under-use the present perfect in English.
contraste.de: In spoken German the Perfekt is the normal past, even with a finished time (Ich habe es gestern gekauft), which leads to I have bought it yesterday. German also uses the present with seit for something still going on, which leads to I live here since 2020.
contraste.it: Italian uses the passato prossimo for finished events (ieri ho visto Marco), which leads to I have seen Marco yesterday. Italian also uses the present with da for something still going on (vivo qui da due anni), which leads to I live here since two years.
contraste.fr: The passé composé is the normal spoken past in French (hier j'ai vu Marc), which leads to I have seen Marc yesterday. French also uses depuis + present for something still going on, which leads to I live here since two years.
contraste.pt: Portuguese uses the simple past for finished events (vi o Marco ontem), which matches the English past simple well. The compound form tenho visto means something repeated up to now and is not the present perfect, and há + present (moro aqui há dois anos) leads to I live here for two years.

errores: Using the present perfect with a finished time word like yesterday.
Using the present perfect after *when*: *When have you arrived?* instead of *When did you arrive?*
Forgetting ever/never with the present perfect for experience.
autochequeo: Does every past simple have a finished time word?
Does every present perfect have an open time, or ever/never?
Is the past simple used after every when question?
Have I used both tenses at least once?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the choice between present perfect and past simple. Check whether each one matches a finished or an open time reference. Do not rewrite the text.

es: *hace dos años que vivo aquí* rendered as *I live here since two years* instead of *I've lived here for two years*.
de: *schon mal* rendered as *already* in experience questions: *Have you already been to Rome?* instead of *Have you ever been to Rome?*
it: *sono qui da due anni* rendered as *I am here since two years* instead of *I've been here for two years*.
fr: *j'habite ici depuis deux ans* rendered as *I live here since two years* instead of *I've lived here for two years*.
pt: *moro aqui há dois anos* rendered with *ago*: *I live here two years ago* instead of *I've lived here for two years*.
